reviews.title: Please include the new example sentences in the reviews!
reviews.text: This has been the most successful method for me to learn kanji. I think I learned over 200 in a matter of 1.5 months. The writing and SRS really works well for me to cement it in my brain. I saw the app recently updated to include example sentences. However, I would love an option to see these sentences already displayed when reviewing a kanji, much like how Anki cards do it, so we’re actively learning the vocab in sentence use without manually navigating to the definition page.

reviews.title: Good but has some issues
reviews.text:
There are plenty of reviews already explaining the pros of this app, which I agree with and are the reasons I give it some stars. There are plenty of issues though:

-Many kanji have no writing practice at all. This becomes more common as you progress.
-The English definitions by themselves don't always indicate whether a verb is transitive/intransitive, such as 延びる and 伸ばす.
-Sometimes you're given a word with 2 valid kanji, like 岡/丘, 路/道, or 探す/捜すand you can't tell which one to write.
-There are a few cases where a kanji is taught in a lesson and used in a compound word with the same meaning, so you don't know which English definition to pick for JP -> EN when they both show up (E.g. 究 is defined as "research, study" and 研究 is "research," 像 is "image" and 画像 is "image, picture").
-The male pronunciation is not available for all words.
-There is a noticeable delay when writing the first stroke.

Overall it's a good app and I don't regret paying for it, but it could use some fixes.

reviews.title: Best Kanji App Out There
reviews.text: This app single handedly has all you need to learn Kanji. SRS review system, learning Kanji through vocab, stroke order practice, in app calendar and reminders, kanji readings/definitions, clearly thought out interface???? It’s all right here. For the cohesiveness and price of the app I’d say this is even better than the big websites like WaniKani. Honestly the only thing I can think of that would improve the app is to add a section to learn radicals, but imo, radicals aren’t necessary; however, they will speed up your kanji learning and improve the effectiveness of this app. If anyone’s reading this, I suggest looking into radicals and seeing if you want to go down that route, if yes, I highly suggest just finding a simple radical anki deck and learning 2, 3, 4 radicals a day alongside this app!

As a Japanese person who didn’t grow up speaking it, but being surrounded by language through family and frequent visits, I find this app helps me learn kanji really well.

The only effective way to learn kanji is to just practicing reading, writing and reviewing them, and I really love how this app introduces new kanji to study and practice.

I use a notepad on the side to further practicing my writing and drilling, but I ways find myself learning and understanding why the kanji build up the way they do. 

This app does a good job at building up the complexity by introducing base kanji before hand.

reviews.title: Great and even better now
reviews.text:
I’ve used this for over 3 years for study now and it’s helped a lot. More importantly there were recent updates that added 1. guidelines (4 small boxes similar to grid writing paper) which can be disabled, for kanji drawing. AND 2. the ability to select “self grading” for English/Japanese translations, meaning it’ll ask you how to read the Kanji(or kanji combination/word) in hiragana, and in English, and then you just select if you got it right or wrong like other flash card apps. This is different than the old way which used to be just show you the kanji and then multiple choice, which meant you were shown a kanji like 勉強　and then given 4 hiragana writings to choose from. Same for English (you’d be given 4 English phrases/words to choose from). I think this is so much better for learning and retention and instead of  “guessing” your way through lessons you really have to think, memorize, and challenge yourself. You can still select multiple choice though if you want.

You can select kanji to review, which reviews all readings you’ve learned. It also has a lookup/lesson grid that allows you view the kanji and their common words, which that alone is like a nice dictionary. It can’t be looked up via stroke count, but you can type the kanji or kana reading on the search bar. And the lessons are nicely organized and broken up by JLPT levels too.

The self review is nice but I’m never sure how well those work in general. I’ve passed my N4 test this last year and I obviously study a lot of different material but I still consistently use this app and I know it’s helped reinforce kanji readings and recognition.
